questions: Are your hand and arm movements involuntary?
Did these movements begin suddenly?
Can you stop the movements briefly when you try?
Are the movements present in both arms?
Are they worse when you hold your arms out or use your hands?
Do the movements disappear when you are asleep?
Have you had any weakness or clumsiness on one side?
Have you had numbness or tingling in your face, arm, or leg?
Have you had trouble speaking, understanding speech, seeing, or walking?
Have you had a severe or unusual headache?
Have you lost awareness, blacked out, or felt confused during an episode?
Have you had any jerking of your legs or whole body?
Have you bitten your tongue or lost bladder control during these episodes?
Have you had similar movements before?
Did they begin after starting or changing a medication?
Have you recently taken medicines for nausea, psychiatric symptoms, pain, sleep, or seizures?
Have you recently stopped alcohol, sedatives, or another regularly used drug?
Have you used recreational drugs or large amounts of caffeine recently?
Do you have a fever or recent infection?
Do you have diabetes or problems with your blood sugar?
Do you have kidney, liver, or thyroid disease?
Have you recently had surgery, anesthesia, or a significant medical illness?
Have you had a recent head injury or stroke?
Do the movements interfere with eating, writing, or holding objects?
Are the movements painful?

dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Bilateral diabetic striatopathy (hyperglycemia-induced chorea/ballism with parkinsonian features) due to severe nonketotic hyperglycemia

ALTERNATIVE 1: Hyperglycemia-associated bilateral striatal injury (nonketotic hyperglycemic basal-ganglia syndrome)

ALTERNATIVE 2: Infection-triggered exacerbation of hyperglycemia-induced movement disorder, likely urinary-tract infection

ALTERNATIVE 3: Atypical bilateral striatal encephalopathy from an underlying toxic–metabolic cause
order_raw:
1. Bedside neurological examination, including characterization of the movements at rest, with posture, during action, and during distraction; assessment for rigidity, bradykinesia, dystonia, chorea, and asterixis
2. Immediate capillary blood glucose
3. Serum glucose, electrolytes, bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, urea, creatinine, and measured serum osmolality
4. Blood ketones and venous blood gas
5. Complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and blood cultures
6. Liver-function tests and ammonia
7. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine
8. Urinalysis and urine ketones
9. Noncontrast CT of the head
10. MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted, susceptibility-weighted, and T1/T2/FLAIR sequences, focusing on the basal ganglia
11. Electroencephalogram
dx: Bilateral diabetic striatopathy (hyperglycemia-induced chorea/ballism with parkinsonian features) due to severe nonketotic hyperglycemia
